item.title: The inventory you own but can't sell
item.description:
ASICS America used to hold back 12 to 15 of every 100 units from its online marketplace feeds because it didn't fully trust the count. Monthly drone counts in its riskiest storage areas let it publish the full feed. The cheapest inventory to add, it turns out, is the inventory you already have.

Four stories from the last few days, from a warehouse that stopped hiding its own stock to power chips booked years ahead, across warehousing, procurement and manufacturing. Every item links to the original source; summaries are our own.
Top storyWarehousingAI in supply chain

1. ASICS finds misplaced stock about 60% faster with nightly drone counts

Twice a year became monthly. ASICS America says autonomous inventory drones from Corvus Robotics now count two of the highest-risk storage areas in its 855,000-square-foot distribution center in Byhalia, Mississippi, every month, a sixfold jump in counting frequency. ASICS reports recovering misplaced inventory about 60% faster and moving about 200 hours a month of counting labor into research and exception work. In one three-month stretch the drones found 26 misplaced cases holding more than 200 pairs of shoes. The figures come from ASICS and Corvus, announced November 10; neither disclosed a price or fleet size. The part supply chain managers should notice is the revenue side. Before the drones, ASICS held back 12 to 15 units of every 100 from its marketplace availability feeds because of fulfillment risk. It now publishes the full feed and sells that product at full price. Why it matters: inventory you can't trust is inventory you can't sell, and the fix started with counting the messiest areas more often, not the whole building.

So what for supply chain managersFind the storage areas where your counts miss most and where stock is held back from sale, then count those more often first.

What to do next
  1. Pull last quarter's cycle count results and rank storage areas or location types by miss rate and by the value of the variances.
  2. Ask sales or e-commerce how many units they hold back from availability feeds or promise dates because they don't trust the count, and in which areas.
  3. Pick the worst one or two areas and test a higher count frequency (manual, scanner or drone) for 60 days before you decide on automation.
You are an inventory control analyst deciding where more frequent cycle counts would pay off. Inputs, anonymized, one row per count: storage area or location type (Area A/B/C), item code, system quantity, counted quantity, unit cost, count date, and whether the item is held back from sale or promise dates (yes/no).
[PASTE TABLE]
1) For each area, calculate the miss rate (counts where system and counted quantity differ, divided by total counts) and the absolute variance value (sum of |counted - system| x unit cost).
2) Rank the areas by absolute variance value, then by miss rate.
3) For the top three areas, name the most common variance pattern (shortage, overage, item found in a wrong location) and flag any items also marked as held back from sale.
4) Suggest a count frequency for each top area (weekly, monthly or quarterly) and estimate the counts per month it adds.
Output: a table with columns area, counts, miss rate, absolute variance value, main pattern, held-back items, suggested frequency, counts per month. Keep it under 300 words. Use only the numbers I give. List any missing or inconsistent data instead of guessing.
#warehouse automation#robotics#AI adoption

Sources: Corvus Robotics announcement: ASICS America recovers misplaced inventory 60% faster Company announcement · Corvus Robotics, ASICS America case study Company announcement · FreightWaves Independent reporting · Robotics & Automation News Independent reporting · Post on X: x.com/FreightWaves/status/2120206856442265872 Post on X

Tip of the DayFor Supply chain managers

Have AI lay out a messy decision as a one-page options memo

When a decision lands on your desk at 4:45 on a Friday, the slow part is laying out the options fairly, not the typing. Paste the facts you have, with supplier, customer and site names swapped for codes, and ask your approved AI tool for options, costs, risks and what each one needs from other teams. It drafts the memo; you check every number against your own data and make the call.

You are an analyst drafting a one-page decision memo for a supply chain manager. Inputs, anonymized (codes instead of supplier, customer and site names): the decision to make, the deadline, the facts and numbers available, constraints (budget, capacity, contract terms) and who is affected.
[PASTE FACTS]
Decision: [DECISION IN ONE SENTENCE]  Deadline: [DATE]
1) Restate the decision and the deadline in one line.
2) Lay out 2 to 4 realistic options, including doing nothing.
3) For each option, give the cost or savings (only from the numbers given), the service and risk impact, what it needs from other teams, and whether it can be reversed.
4) Recommend one option and say what new information would change the recommendation.
Output: a short memo with one heading per step, plus a table with columns option, cost impact, service impact, main risk, needs from others, reversible (yes/no). Keep it under 350 words. Use anonymized data only. List any missing or inconsistent data instead of guessing.

2. Infineon expects data-center power chip sales to nearly double, backed by over €10 billion in capacity deals

Over €10 billion. That's the combined revenue volume of multi-year supply and capacity reservation agreements, signed or still under negotiation, that Infineon says customers have lined up for its data-center power products. The chipmaker said on November 10 that revenue from power supplies for AI and conventional data centers should reach close to €4 billion in fiscal 2027, up from €2.2 billion. CEO Jochen Hanebeck said Infineon could not meet all customer requests in fiscal 2026, even after ramping production.

More than 9,000 robots, and now a layer meant to run them as one team. DHL Supply Chain said on November 9 that, after a proof of concept, it is deploying AI orchestration in live warehouse operations as a digital control center connecting site data, employees and automated equipment. It is also piloting adaptive robots that work toward a goal instead of following a fixed route. DHL did not publish throughput or cost results for the orchestration layer.

4. Path Robotics raises $300 million to take AI welding beyond the weld

$300 million at a $2.45 billion valuation. Path Robotics, which builds AI-guided welding robots, announced the Series E led by Georgian on November 10. Its Obsidian model watches parts warp from heat during welding and adjusts as it goes, which is where robots running a fixed program tend to struggle, SiliconANGLE reported. CEO Andy Lonsberry said manufacturers that need more capacity "can't get there with traditional automation," and the company plans to take on the tasks before and after welding next.

So what for operations and plant managersIf welding is a bottleneck in your supply base, ask your fabrication suppliers whether AI-guided cells are in their capacity plans and how much part variation they handle.

item.title: What your AI tools can see, and who else might
item.description:
One in six supply chain, logistics and distribution managers in a new InstaLILY survey say an AI tool exposed, shared or wrongly accessed supplier or customer data in the past year. In logistics, that can mean a carrier rate turning up in a customer quote. Find out what your AI tools can see before a customer does.

Four stories from the past week, from a survey on AI and confidential rates to this morning's Taiwan trade numbers, across freight, warehousing and trade. Every item links to the original source; summaries are our own.
Top storyLogisticsAI in supply chain

1. One in six supply chain leaders say an AI tool exposed supplier or customer data

One in six. That's the share of 250 supply chain, logistics, distribution and wholesale managers who told InstaLILY their company had an incident in the past year in which supplier or customer data was exposed, shared or accessed incorrectly through an AI tool. The AI-agent vendor published the survey on November 4. The reach is wide: 78% say their AI tools can access customer pricing and margins, and 67% say the same for supplier pricing and rebate data. Even so, 87% are very or somewhat confident their AI keeps that data separated. The results are self-reported, and the survey does not measure how serious the incidents were. Why it matters: logistics teams sit on both sides of the deal. InstaLILY's own example is an AI tool showing a shipper the carrier rate behind a broker's margin. With peak season adding quotes and rate requests, it's a good week to check what your AI tools can see and test whether they repeat it.

So what for logistics leadsMap which AI tools can read carrier rates and customer prices, then test one quote per tool before peak volume hits.

What to do next
  1. List every AI tool your team uses, including AI features inside your TMS, WMS and email, and note which ones can read carrier rates, customer prices, margins or rebates.
  2. Run one test per tool: have it draft a customer quote or rate reply, and check whether any carrier cost, margin or other customer's terms show up.
  3. Write down which AI replies need a human approval before they reach a customer or carrier, and send the list to whoever owns each tool.
You are a logistics operations analyst mapping what our AI tools can see. Inputs, anonymized, one row per tool: tool code (Tool A/B/C), where it runs (TMS, WMS, email, chat, spreadsheet add-in), data it can read (carrier rates, customer prices, margins, rebates, shipment details), who can use it, and whether its output reaches customers or carriers without review (yes/no).
[PASTE TABLE]
1) Flag every tool that can read both cost-side data (carrier rates, supplier rebates) and customer-facing data (customer prices, quotes).
2) For each flagged tool, write one test request that could pull cost data into a customer reply (for example, "draft a quote for lane [LANE CODE]").
3) Rank the tools by risk: output sent without review first, then the number of sensitive data types each can read.
4) For the top three, say where a human approval step should sit.
Output: a table with columns tool, sensitive data it can read, output reviewed (yes/no), risk rank, test request, approval point. Keep it under 300 words. Use anonymized data only. List any missing or inconsistent data instead of guessing.
#AI adoption#pricing#freight

Tip of the DayFor Logistics and warehouse teams

Have AI turn your SOPs into checklists for peak-season hires

Peak brings new faces to the dock, and nobody reads a 12-page SOP on day one. Paste one procedure (site names and customer details removed) into your approved AI tool and ask for a short numbered checklist with the safety and quality steps marked. Then walk it with a lead on the floor before you print it: the AI drafts, the floor corrects.

You are a warehouse training lead turning a procedure into a checklist for new seasonal staff. Input: one standard operating procedure, anonymized, with site names, customer names and system passwords removed.
[PASTE SOP TEXT]
The checklist is for: [NEW PICKER / RECEIVER / LOADER]
1) Rewrite the procedure as a numbered checklist of no more than [15] steps, one action per step, in plain words.
2) Mark every safety step with [SAFETY] and every step where a mistake causes a quality or inventory error with [CHECK].
3) List any step in the SOP that is unclear, out of order, or missing a tool, scanner screen or approval.
4) Add three questions a supervisor can ask to confirm the new hire understood.
Output: the checklist, then the unclear-steps list, then the three questions. Keep it under 300 words. Use anonymized data only. List any missing or inconsistent data instead of guessing.

2. GXO's AI flags replenishment before the pick face runs dry

Before the pick location runs out, not when it does. GXO says a tool it demonstrated for a fashion retail customer uses historical ordering patterns to flag when to replenish ahead of a stockout. CEO Patrick Kelleher told Logistics Management that GXO IQ, its AI middleware and data lake, is on track for more than 50 operations this year, and that GXO goes into peak with about 25% more seasonal headcount than last year. GXO reported third-quarter results on November 3.

3. Kodiak's driverless trucks double their freight as IKEA Supply lines up for long-haul

More than 396,000 tons in one quarter, over double the quarter before. That's how much freight Kodiak AI's autonomous trucks moved in the third quarter, the company said on November 5. It named IKEA Supply as its first launch partner for unsupervised long-haul service, starting on the Dallas-to-Houston corridor, and says its internal Autonomy Readiness Measure has reached 99% ahead of a targeted year-end launch. Kodiak has passed 58,000 paid driverless hours and nearly 30,000 loads.

4. Taiwan's exports hit a record $96.76 billion on AI demand as Asia air space tightens

US$96.76 billion, up 58.9% from a year earlier. Taiwan's Ministry of Finance said on Monday that October exports set a monthly record, and it credited heavy investment in AI infrastructure. Shipments to the U.S. rose 55.9% to a record US$32.93 billion, CNA's Focus Taiwan reported, and the ministry expects US$94.2 billion to US$96.7 billion in November. C.H. Robinson's November air update says servers, chip equipment and data-center components from Taiwan and nearby origins are tightening trans-Pacific capacity, with Asia-origin rates expected to rise through November.

So what for plannersIf Asia-made electronics or data-center parts are on your inbound plan, add air booking lead time now and flag which lines could move by ocean instead.

item.title: Electrical gear leads stretch on AI power demand
item.description:
Eaton's rolling 12-month data-center orders rose more than 100%, and CEO Paulo Ruiz said demand "continues to run ahead of what we can convert." Generac's data-center generator backlog is about $4.5 billion after its Amazon deal. If switchgear or backup power sits on your open PO list, treat this week's lead-time check as non-optional.

Four stories from the last few days, across electrical gear for data centers, backup generators, electronics BOM tools and warehouse autonomy. Every item links to the original source; summaries are our own.
Top storyProcurementSupply chain for AI

1. Eaton data-center orders more than double as electrical demand outruns new capacity

More than 100% growth in rolling 12-month data-center orders. That's what Eaton reported on its November 3 earnings call, alongside data-center revenue up about 65% and a ninth straight quarter of data-center growth above 35%. CEO Paulo Ruiz said Electrical Americas backlog is up 33% and "demand continues to run ahead of what we can convert," even as organic sales in that segment rose 22%. Electrical book-to-bill sat at 1.2, with Americas at 1.3, and total electrical backlog above $20 billion, up 46% year over year. The company also announced general price increases for Electrical Americas and Global effective January 2, 2027. Why it matters: AI data-center buildouts are pulling the same switchgear, UPS and distribution gear plants and warehouses buy for everyday work. Materials managers with electrical lines on open POs or 2027 capital plans may be working from lead times and quotes that no longer hold.

So what for materials managersRe-check lead times and quote validity on electrical gear this week, and escalate any line that slipped more than two weeks.

What to do next
  1. Export open POs and planned buys for switchgear, UPS, breakers, transformers and related electrical gear, with supplier, qty, promise date and quote date.
  2. Ask each supplier for current standard lead time, expedite options and how long today's quote stays valid, especially into first-half 2027.
  3. Flag any quote older than 30 days or any promise date that moved out more than two weeks, and decide which lines to firm with a blanket PO or alternate source.
You are a materials manager checking whether electrical-gear lead times and quotes still match your open work. Inputs, anonymized, one row per line: item code, description (switchgear/UPS/breaker/other), supplier code, open qty, promise date, quote date, quoted unit price, planned need date.
[PASTE TABLE]
Today's date: [DATE]
1) Flag every line whose quote is older than [30] days or whose promise date is after the planned need date.
2) Flag every line where the promise date has slipped more than [14] days versus the original need date (note the gap in days).
3) Rank flagged lines by open qty times quoted unit price and mark the top ten to call first.
4) Draft three short questions to ask each supplier about current lead time, expedite options and quote validity into [FIRST HALF 2027].
Output: a table with columns item code, supplier code, open qty, quote age days, slip days, extended value, action; then the questions. Keep it under 300 words. Use anonymized data only. List any missing or inconsistent data instead of guessing.
#data centers#lead times#AI hardware#pricing

Sources: Eaton third quarter 2026 results Company announcement · The Motley Fool, Eaton Q3 2026 earnings call transcript Independent reporting · Post on X: x.com/AlphaAllocators/status/2117703651104084231 Post on X

Tip of the DayFor Material managers

Have AI rank your expedite list from open POs and shortages

Expedite calls eat the morning when every past-due line looks urgent. Export open purchase orders and the shortage or MRP exception list for one planner, anonymized, and have your approved AI tool score each line by days late, shortage risk and extended value. It drafts the call order; you still decide who gets a phone call and who gets an email.

You are a materials manager building today's expedite call list. Inputs, anonymized: (a) open POs, one row per line: PO number, item code, supplier code, open qty, promise date, unit price; (b) shortages or MRP exceptions, one row per item: item code, shortage qty, need date, customer or work-order code.
[PASTE OPEN POS]
[PASTE SHORTAGES]
Today's date: [DATE]
1) Join the two lists on item code. Flag every open PO line that covers a shortage or is already past the promise date.
2) Score each flagged line: days late (or days until need date if not late), shortage qty, and extended value (open qty times unit price).
3) Rank by a simple priority: shortages first, then days late, then extended value. List the top fifteen to work today.
4) Draft a two-sentence expedite note template with blanks for promise date and ship method.
Output: a table with columns priority, PO number, item code, supplier code, days late, shortage qty, extended value, suggested action; then the note template. Keep it under 300 words. Use anonymized data only. List any missing or inconsistent data instead of guessing.

item.title: Memory costs reach the warehouse floor
item.description:
Zebra Technologies raised prices on its mobile computers by about 15% in October to cover extra memory costs it now puts at $145 million for the year. It expects memory to keep getting pricier into the first half of 2027. If a scanner refresh is in your 2027 plan, that September quote is already a collector's item.

Four stories from the last two days, across device costs, planning software, air freight and warehouse robots. Plus a new worked safety stock example in Guides. Every item links to the original source; summaries are our own.
Top storyProcurementSupply chain for AI

1. Zebra raises mobile computer prices about 15% as memory costs climb toward $145 million

About 15% more for a handheld computer. That's what Zebra Technologies' October price increase adds across its mobile computing products, CFO Nathan Winters said on the company's November 3 earnings call. The reason is memory. Zebra now expects memory components to cost it about $145 million more this year, up from an earlier estimate of $120 million, and said memory costs rose more than $50 million year over year in the third quarter alone, with price increases covering about half. Winters expects memory prices to keep rising into the first half of 2027 before easing in the second half. Zebra is hedging too: inventory rose about $90 million in the quarter, mostly from stocking memory ahead, and it has qualified five new memory suppliers. Why it matters: memory costs are no longer just a server problem. Buyers and planners with scanner, mobile computer or other memory-heavy device refreshes in their 2027 budgets may be working from prices that no longer apply.

So what for buyersRequote memory-heavy devices in your 2027 plan now, and ask suppliers how long they will hold today's price.

What to do next
  1. List the scanners, mobile computers, printers and other memory-heavy devices in your 2027 plan, and ask suppliers to requote anything priced before October.
  2. Ask each device supplier how long its quotes are valid and whether it will hold price on a firm order or blanket PO for first-half 2027 deliveries.
  3. For refreshes that can wait, compare the cost of ordering now with waiting for the second-half 2027 easing Zebra expects, and write down the assumption you used.
You are a buyer checking how rising memory costs affect next year's device purchases. Inputs, anonymized, one row per planned purchase: device type, supplier code, quantity, quoted unit price, quote date, quote valid until, planned order month, planned delivery month.
[PASTE TABLE]
Assumed price increase for quotes dated before [DATE]: [X%]
1) Flag every line whose quote is dated before [DATE] or expires before the planned order month.
2) For flagged lines, calculate the budget at the assumed increase and the dollar difference.
3) Rank lines by dollar difference and mark the top five to requote first.
4) Draft three short questions to ask each supplier about price holds, quote validity and delivery dates.
Output: a table with columns device type, supplier code, quantity, quoted total, adjusted total, difference, action; then the questions. Keep it under 300 words. Use anonymized data only. List any missing or inconsistent data instead of guessing.
#memory#pricing#warehouse automation

Sources: Zebra Technologies third quarter 2026 results Company announcement · The Motley Fool, Zebra Q3 2026 earnings call transcript Independent reporting · TipRanks Independent reporting · Post on X: x.com/Finsee_main/status/2117626833701130473 Post on X

Tip of the DayFor Planners

Have AI find the safety stocks still running on old lead times

Safety stock goes stale when the lead time in your system stops matching the lead time at your dock, and many of those settings were typed in during a calmer year. Export recent receipts and the planning parameters for one item group, anonymized, and have your approved AI tool compare planned and actual lead times item by item. It flags the gaps; you check a couple of rows by hand and decide which settings to change.

You are an inventory planner checking whether planning lead times still match reality. Inputs, anonymized: (a) planning parameters, one row per item: item code, planned lead time (days), safety stock (units), average daily demand (units); (b) receipts from the last [6] months, one row per receipt: item code, PO date, receipt date.
[PASTE PARAMETERS]
[PASTE RECEIPTS]
1) For each item, calculate actual lead time per receipt (receipt date minus PO date), then the average and standard deviation.
2) Flag items where the average actual lead time differs from the planned lead time by more than [20%] or [5] days.
3) For flagged items, estimate how many days of demand the current safety stock covers against the gap.
4) Rank flagged items by the gap in days and list the top ten to review first.
Output: a table with columns item code, planned lead time, actual average, actual standard deviation, gap (days), safety stock days of cover, action; then the top ten. Keep it under 300 words. Use anonymized data only, and don't change any setting without your own review. List any missing or inconsistent data instead of guessing.

4. Tutor Intelligence raises $75 million to rent out warehouse robots by the hour

No upfront purchase, no long-term contract. Tutor Intelligence charges for its robots by the hour or by the pick, and on November 2 it announced a $75 million Series B led by Andreessen Horowitz, bringing its total raised to $117 million. Its single-arm Cassie robot handles case picking and palletizing, while two-armed Sonny does finer e-commerce picking; remote human operators guide both as they learn. The company says its robots now work in almost four times as many facilities as a year ago, and it targets more than 1,000 robots under contract by the end of 2027.

So what for warehouse managersIf capital approval keeps automation off your floor, ask robot vendors for per-hour or per-pick pricing and compare it with your fully loaded cost per pick.

item.title: Three trade clocks run out the same week
item.description:
All 178 remaining Section 301 tariff exclusions on Chinese goods expire at 11:59 p.m. ET on November 9, and as of November 1 no extension had been published. The U.S. pause on China port fees ends the same night. Expect your customs broker's phone to be busy this week.

Four stories since Friday, across trade, data-center financing, freight billing and factory robots. Every item links to the original source; summaries are our own.
Top storyTradeAI in supply chain

1. 178 tariff exclusions, U.S. port fees and China's export-control pause all hit their end dates the week of November 9

One week, three expiry dates. All 178 remaining Section 301 product exclusions on Chinese goods end at 11:59 p.m. ET on November 9 under the extension USTR published in December 2025, and the International Compliance Professionals Association's tracker said on November 1 that no notice extending them had been published. Goods entered on or after November 10 that relied on an exclusion would pay the full List rate, which runs from 7.5% to 25%. item.title: Thieves are hijacking data center freight
item.description:
Thieves have taken more than $100 million in data center freight off U.S. highways since June, NBC News reports, often by first taking over freight broker accounts. If you ship servers, memory or power gear, checking who actually picks up the load is now part of the buy.

Top storyLogisticsSupply chain for AI

1. Thieves have stolen more than $100 million in data center freight since June

More than $100 million. That's how much data center cargo thieves have taken off U.S. highways since June, NBC News reported on October 26, based on accounts from industry executives, consultants and investigators who advise police. Targets include servers, memory chips, fiber-optic cable, copper wire and data center power and cooling gear. In early June, a trailer with about $13 million in server equipment headed for Fayetteville, Georgia, was among the losses. The method is mostly digital: thieves take over freight broker accounts on load boards, post fake loads, send malware links to carriers that respond, then use those carriers' accounts to bid on real shipments. Some use fake driver's licenses, and in one large theft the tracking signal was spoofed. Scott Cornell, chair of TAPA Americas, told FreightWaves in August that two escorted loads were lost after escorts were deliberately hit, and he tied both to drivers who weren't properly vetted. Why it matters: the weak point is carrier and driver verification, which buyers and logistics teams can check before the load moves.

So what for logistics leadsFor every high-value AI hardware shipment in the next 60 days, confirm in writing how the carrier and driver are verified at pickup, and treat any emailed change to pickup details as suspect until confirmed by phone.

What to do next

item.title: Most supply chain teams aren't ready for their AI
item.description:
83% of supply chain leaders in a new ASCM and DSCI survey say their employees aren't ready to use AI effectively. The tools are moving faster than the people using them, so this week's most useful AI project may be training the team on one process, not buying another agent.

Of 107 qualified respondents, 83% said their employees are unprepared to use AI well, and 64% of the unprepared group is still stuck in pilots or planning. On a scale from 1 (no AI) to 5 (fully autonomous), adoption across 13 supply chain functions averaged 1.94. Demand planning led at 2.28; reverse logistics was last at 1.59. The top barriers tied at 33% each: missing skills and an unclear business case. Why it matters: involvement drops off below the top. 82% of C-suite respondents lead or scale AI work, but 70% of staff say they're aware of it without being involved. The people who run the process aren't helping shape the tool.

So what for supply chain managersPick one process your team runs every week, measure how it works today, and get the people who do the work involved before anyone buys another AI tool for it.

When a new order arrives, the agent generates several production scenarios, shows planners how each one scores on defined KPIs, and checks the proposals against a digital twin of the whole plant before anything changes on the floor. item.title: Free forecasting models pass a grocery test
item.description:
In an independent grocery test, Mistral's new Timestral and Google's TimesFM made 4.5% to 6.3% less forecast error than a classic statistical method, with no training on the data. A modern forecasting model is now worth an afternoon backtest. Just read the license before you fall in love.

Five stories from the past week across planning, procurement, freight, trade and warehousing. Every item links to the original source; summaries are our own.
Top storyPlanningAI in supply chain

1. Free AI forecasting models just beat a classic method on grocery data

4.5% to 6.3% less forecast error, with no training on the data. That's what Superlinear found when it tested Mistral's new Timestral models and Google's TimesFM against ETS, a classic statistical method many planning systems still rely on, using Walmart M5 food sales and a fresh-food dataset. Mistral released Timestral on October 15: four open-weight time-series models, from 5 million to 209 million parameters, that produce probabilistic forecasts, accept known future inputs such as planned promotions, and run on an ordinary CPU. In Superlinear's test, the small 28M version came within 0.4% of the largest model's accuracy in about a fifth of the time. Two cautions: Superlinear says Timestral is free only for companies under $20 million in monthly revenue, and it advises judging a forecast on service level, waste and stock, not error alone.

So what for plannersYou can test a modern forecasting model against your current numbers on your own history without buying anything. Run a small, anonymized backtest before your next S&OP cycle, and judge it on bias and service level, not only error.

What to do next
  1. Pick 50 to 100 anonymized items with at least two years of weekly history, hold out the last 12 weeks, and compare an open model's forecast with your current system's.
  2. Score both on bias, service level and stock, not just forecast error, and look separately at promo weeks and slow movers.
  3. Have IT or legal check the model's license and your company's AI policy before any real data or production use.

Have AI flag every exception hiding in a supplier quote

Suppliers often accept your RFQ on page one and take exceptions in the fine print: price-adjustment clauses, bigger minimums, longer lead times, different Incoterms. 2. Microsoft walks away from the UK's biggest planned AI data center over power

No grid power until the 2030s: that's what Nscale was told about its planned data center in Loughton, Essex, which was meant to house about 23,000 Nvidia chips and open next year. Microsoft, its only publicly announced customer for the site, has ended its agreement, the BBC and the Guardian reported on October 18; Microsoft declined to comment. Nscale says it remains committed, is exploring alternative power sources, and that its Microsoft projects in Norway, Portugal and the US are unaffected.

So what for procurement leadersA signed AI capacity deal is only as firm as the site's power connection. item.title: The memory crunch sinks phone shipments, Taiwan moves to criminalize AI chip smuggling, and Amazon keeps shutting out shopping agents
item.description:
Six stories from the past week across planning, trade, manufacturing, freight, warehousing and sourcing. Every item links to the original source; summaries are our own.
PlanningSupply chain for AI

1. AI's appetite for memory just caused the worst quarter on record for smartphones

IDC's preliminary numbers show global smartphone shipments fell 22% year over year in the third quarter to about 255 million units, the steepest quarterly drop it has ever recorded. IDC blames the AI-driven memory shortage: memory costs are up roughly 350% from a year ago, and vendors have cut low-end models and raised prices. IDC expects pressure to last through 2027 and warns that some makers built ahead of next year's expected component squeeze, which could leave excess inventory if demand stays soft.

So what for plannersIf any of your products use DRAM or flash, treat memory as a constrained, fast-moving cost input in your plan. Re-run 2027 demand and cost scenarios with current memory pricing, watch for customers pulling back on budget models, and be careful not to build inventory ahead of a squeeze that weak demand may never absorb.

#memory#chips#data centers#forecasting

Sources: 9to5Mac Independent reporting · Mobile World Live Independent reporting · FoneArena Independent reporting

TradeSupply chain for AI

2. Taiwan plans to make unauthorized AI chip shipments to China a crime

Taiwan's economics minister, Kung Ming-hsin, told Bloomberg that Taipei will add AI servers and leading-edge semiconductors to its list of controlled goods, in line with commitments under its trade agreement with the US. Once the change takes effect, shipping restricted AI hardware to China without authorization would become a criminal offense under Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act. Today, Taiwan can only pursue suspected smugglers under other laws. No start date has been given.

So what for trade compliance teamsExpect tighter screening on AI servers and accelerators that ship from or through Taiwan. Check that your end-use and end-user documentation for this hardware is complete, ask your distributors how they plan to comply, and build some extra lead time into orders while the new rules are being set up.

#export controls#chips

Sources: Bloomberg Independent reporting · The Straits Times Independent reporting

ManufacturingSupply chain for AI

3. Adani and Jabil sign up to build AI racks and servers in India

Adani Enterprises and contract manufacturer Jabil signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding on October 13 for a 50:50 joint venture to make and assemble AI racks, servers, storage, networking gear, power distribution, liquid cooling and transformers in India, plus installation and commissioning. The companies are aiming for multi-gigawatt rack capacity for Indian and export customers. No investment figure or production date was given, and the deal still needs definitive agreements and approvals.

So what for supply chain managersAnother region is lining up to build AI data-center hardware, which could widen your options for racks, power and cooling over time. Note it on your supplier map, but don't count on it as capacity until there's a signed JV, a plant and a qualified product.

#AI hardware#data centers#manufacturing capacity

Sources: Adani Enterprises release Company announcement · CNBC-TV18 Independent reporting · Voice&Data Independent reporting

LogisticsAI in supply chain

4. Kodiak's autonomous trucks now run reefer and dry freight to Laredo

Kodiak AI and carrier Charger Logistics are hauling refrigerated and dry-van freight for food, beverage and consumer-goods shippers on the 435-mile lane between Dallas and Laredo, the busiest US land port of entry. The first load ran September 8, and a safety driver is still on board until Kodiak finishes its safety case. Charger owns the trucks and runs Kodiak's driving system under a driver-as-a-service model, and it has a separate autonomy deal with Aurora on the same lane.

So what for logistics leadsAutonomous capacity is reaching cross-border feeder lanes, not just Dallas to Houston. If you move freight toward Laredo, ask carriers which loads might ride autonomous trucks, how handoffs to Mexican carriers work, and what changes in tracking, liability and service commitments.

#autonomous trucks#freight

Sources: Kodiak AI news release Company announcement · FreightWaves Independent reporting · CCJ Independent reporting

WarehousingAI in supply chain

5. Robots are sorting Zalando's fashion returns without item-by-item training

Sereact's two-armed robots are now sorting Zalando returns in live operations at CEVA Logistics sites in Greven, Germany, and Świebodzin, Poland. Sereact says its Cortex software lets the robots pick, identify and sort crumpled items they've never seen, without per-product setup or a fixed item list. The system is sold as robotics-as-a-service, and staff move to supervising stations, handling exceptions and checking quality. The companies call it the first step toward automating returns across Europe.

So what for warehouse managersReturns are among the hardest jobs to automate, so this is a useful test case. If returns volume is a pain point, ask vendors for live rates on mixed, messy items, what share of items still fall to people, and how pricing works under a service contract.

#robotics#warehouse automation#returns

Sources: Sereact announcement Company announcement · The Next Web Independent reporting · International Transport Journal Independent reporting

ProcurementAI in supply chain

6. Amazon keeps blocking outside AI shopping agents, and now Grok Bot hits the wall

On October 15, users posted screenshots showing xAI's Grok Bot being stopped from ordering on Amazon with a notice that access by an unauthorized AI agent breaks Amazon's Conditions of Use. Elon Musk replied that users could buy elsewhere and floated starting an Amazon competitor, without giving details. Amazon hasn't publicly commented on Grok Bot, but it confirmed last month that it blocked Meta's Muse agent and is fighting Perplexity in court, arguing that agents should identify themselves and get the store's agreement.

So what for procurement leadersAgent-driven buying will depend on which sellers and marketplaces let agents in. Before you pilot AI agents for purchasing, check each supplier's terms on automated ordering, favor channels with official agent or punchout integrations, and keep a person approving orders and payment details.

#AI agents#agentic commerce

Sources: Teslarati Independent reporting · Investing.com Independent reporting · GeekWire (Muse block) Independent reporting

Tip of the DayFor Supply chain managers

Use AI to run a quick what-if on your riskiest single-source parts

Pick the ten items where one supplier or one region would hurt most if it went down. Give your approved AI assistant an anonymized table of those items and ask it to walk through a four-week outage for each: what runs out first, what it costs, and which fallback buys the most time. It won't replace a full risk model, but it turns a vague worry into a ranked list you can act on this quarter.

You are a supply chain risk analyst. Below are our 10 highest-exposure items (anonymized): item code, supplier code, supplier region, weeks of stock on hand, weekly usage, lead time in weeks, whether an alternate source is qualified (Y/N), and margin impact per week of lost output.
[PASTE TABLE]

1) For each item, estimate the week we run out and the total margin at risk. Show your math.
2) Rank the items by margin at risk.
3) For the top 3, suggest two realistic mitigations (for example: buffer stock, qualify an alternate, re-sequence production) and roughly what each would cost or require.
4) List any data that's missing or looks inconsistent instead of guessing.
Use a table for steps 1 and 2. Keep the whole answer under 300 words.

item.title: TSMC says AI chip demand still outruns supply, robot trucks take on routine freight, and robot brains go on tap
item.description:
Eight stories from the past week across freight, warehousing, factories, planning, sourcing and trade. Every item links to the original source; summaries are our own.
ManufacturingSupply chain for AI

1. TSMC: AI chip demand is still bigger than its capacity, and it's scouting Texas

TSMC reported third-quarter revenue of about $46.7B, up roughly 51% from a year ago, and guided fourth-quarter revenue to $52.3B to $54.3B. Management said AI-related demand remains very strong and the gap between demand and supply is still large, with 2026 capital spending planned at $60B to $64B. The WSJ reported that TSMC has sent teams to Texas to evaluate expansion beyond Arizona.

So what for buyersDon't plan on leading-edge chip or advanced-packaging lead times easing in 2027. For anything with AI accelerators or high-end logic inside, keep forecasts current with your distributors, confirm allocation in writing, and ask which builds depend on CoWoS packaging capacity.

#chips#manufacturing capacity#data centers#lead times

2. A Texas carrier adds Waabi's autonomous trucks to haul repeat freight

Warrior Logistics, an asset-based carrier with 200+ trucks, is running recurring food, beverage and consumer-goods loads on Waabi Driver-powered trucks between Dallas and Houston. Waabi says those routes have so far delivered 100% on-time pickup and delivery with no safety incidents, though neither company shared truck or load counts. Waabi also says its load volume on the lane is up more than 80% this year.

Brooklyn-based Ultra closed a $50M Series A led by Framework Ventures, bringing total funding to $62M. It installs its OP1 packing robots at warehouses and third-party logistics sites for an upfront integration fee plus a monthly service fee, rather than a big capital purchase. The company says its robots have packed over 500,000 orders, and it relies on Physical Intelligence for the AI models that run them.

4. Kao's AI agent drafts demand plans, and people still make the call

In an English release this week, Japanese consumer-goods maker Kao detailed Kao-MIKOMIL, an AI agent that layers planned promotions, channels and pricing on top of forecasts from its in-house AI forecasting model, then proposes a demand plan with its reasoning. Business staff review and approve the plan. It went live for the KATE cosmetics brand in July and will expand to other brands, as part of Kao's goal to cut cosmetics inventory about 25% by 2027 versus 2024.

So what for plannersThe useful pattern here is the split: a forecasting model for the baseline, and an AI agent that explains how promotions and launches change it. Ask for the rationale with every AI-suggested plan, and track whether it actually beats your current forecast before you trust it.

5. Samsara opens its no-code AI agent builder to all fleet customers

Samsara made Agent Studio generally available on October 13. Fleets can build chat and voice agents on their own operating data, for example to compile reports, flag possible hours-of-service violations, or answer driver questions from company policy. Samsara says agent use is now running at about seven times its June launch pace, but it hasn't said how many customers run agents in production.

So what for logistics leadsStart with one narrow agent that has a clear owner and a checkable answer, like a daily hours-of-service risk list. Keep a person approving anything that changes a dispatch or touches a driver's record.

6. Physical Intelligence opens its robot models to outside developers

Physical Intelligence launched a waitlisted beta of its Pi API on October 13. Teams upload their own robot data, fine-tune the company's general-purpose models on its managed infrastructure, and run them through a hosted service. Robots-as-a-service provider Formic, which says 150 factories use its robots, is an early partner. The company noted that network connectivity was a challenge in some early cloud-run deployments.

So what for operations and plant managersGeneral-purpose robot AI is becoming something you rent, not build. If you evaluate it, plan for the plant network: test what happens when connectivity drops, where your production data goes, and who owns the fine-tuned model.

7. Scimplify raises $25M to add US capacity for specialty and critical-materials chemistry

Scimplify, a Bengaluru-based specialty chemicals and advanced materials maker, raised $25M in a round led by Hitachi Ventures, with Henkel and Teknor Apex joining. Total funding is now about $80M. It plans US research and processing capacity for areas with thin domestic supply, such as rare-earth and critical-metal purification and high-purity semiconductor and battery chemicals, and will keep building its in-house AI platform for taking chemistry from lab to production.

So what for procurement leadersNew suppliers for hard-to-source chemistries are forming, often backed by the customers who need them. Add players like this to your market scan, but qualify them like any new source: samples, quality systems, and proven capacity before you shift volume.

#funding#critical materials#manufacturing capacity

January's Section 232 tariff put 25% on certain advanced logic chips but exempted chips headed for US data centers, pending a Commerce Department review that hasn't been published. On October 2, five tech trade groups including CCIA and TechNet asked the White House to keep any further chip, robotics and machinery tariffs targeted, and to extend any tariff offset program to downstream buyers. No second-phase decision has been announced.

So what for trade compliance teamsIf you import servers, accelerators or robotics, map which items fall under the current tariff codes and which end-use exemption you rely on. Keep the paperwork for that exemption ready, and model landed cost both with and without it.

Accessorial charges like detention, lumper and liftgate fees are where freight bills quietly drift. Each week, export invoiced charges next to the rate confirmation for the same loads, swap carrier and customer names for neutral codes, and have your approved AI assistant flag every mismatch. item.title: AI hardware is sold out, agents are learning to shop, and the financing bill is coming due

The CEO of optical-components maker Lumentum told Bloomberg the company is fully booked into early 2029. For some product lines, it can't fill about 70% of demand through 2027, and some customers are already placing orders for 2030. Six months ago, he expected to sell out only through 2028.

So what for buyersIf you buy networking or server hardware, ask distributors now about allocation and lead times on anything with high-speed optics. Put forecasts in early, and get second-source quotes before a 52-week lead time lands on you.

Bloomberg put the figure nearer $30B and called the talks early. Either way, private credit is now funding chip supply directly.
